screens.title: Deployment Models & First Steps for Cisco SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the choices and early steps that make a Cisco SD‑WAN deployment work. You will learn the tradeoffs between on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, and hybrid controller models, and you will see why controller placement and sizing are practical design decisions, not abstract concepts. We will also walk through the initial vManage virtual machine configuration and the certificate and licensing steps that let controllers and edges form a secure fabric. A concrete example you will encounter is placing vBond in a public cloud to make it reachable by NATed branch devices while keeping vManage inside a private data center for control and monitoring. Common mistakes like unsynchronized clocks, blocked firewall ports, and duplicate system IPs are shown along with how they disrupt trust and device joins. By the end of this chapter you will be able to pick an appropriate deployment model for a given organizational constraint, perform the initial vManage CLI setup, request and install certificates, and add vBond and vSmart into the fabric. Ask yourself: which constraint in your environment makes control plane placement the highest priority?

screens.title: Deployment Models: On‑Premises, Cloud‑Hosted, Hybrid
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment model selection is the first architectural decision for SD‑WAN controllers and it shapes operational, security, and availability tradeoffs. An on‑premises deployment places vManage, vSmart, and vBond on servers you control in your data center. This gives maximum control and data sovereignty and is sensible where an organization already has robust virtualization and prefers to own its infrastructure. A concrete example: a global enterprise with two main data centers that wants to avoid public cloud dependency will host all controllers on‑premises, leveraging existing virtualization and backup processes. The cloud‑hosted model moves controllers to public cloud VMs. This offers elasticity, managed availability, and reduced hardware operations. For instance, placing vBond or vManage in a cloud region reduces administrative hardware tasks and can simplify reachability for widely dispersed branches. Hybrid mixes both: keep sensitive controllers in your own DC while placing vBond in the cloud to help NATed branch devices find and register with the fabric. A common misconception is that cloud always means better redundancy; in reality, cloud reduces physical hardware management but still requires correct placement and architecture for low latency and regulatory compliance. Takeaway: match the model to control, reachability, and operational skillsets, not to a single buzzword.

keyIdea.text: On‑premises gives control, cloud-hosted offers scalability, and hybrid combines them to balance reachability and sovereignty.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Deployment Models
Core Concept

Deployment models explained

Three approaches—on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, hybrid—each trade control, reachability, and operations differently.

On‑Premises
Max control and data sovereignty. Requires you to manage physical or virtual servers and networking.
Cloud‑Hosted
Deploy controllers as VMs in public clouds for scalability and managed availability but consider latency.
Hybrid
Combine on‑premises and cloud to keep sensitive data local while ensuring reachability for NATed edges.
Example Scenarios
Global enterprise with existing DCs
Likely on‑premises: leverages virtualization and keeps control of data and backups.
Cloud‑centric operator
Cloud‑hosted controllers reduce hardware ops and improve rapid scaling during growth.
Hybrid use case
Keep vManage in DC, place vBond in public cloud to allow NATed branches to register easily.
Key Takeaway

Choose the model that aligns with your control, compliance, and reachability needs. Cloud availability doesn't remove design work for latency and security.

screens.title: On‑Premises Deployment: Strengths and Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: On‑premises deployments are chosen when control, privacy, and tight integration with existing infrastructure are priorities. By installing vManage, vSmart, and vBond inside your own data centers you control patching windows, backup strategies, and network segmentation. A practical example is an enterprise that must retain logs and telemetry within its own environment for compliance; hosting controllers locally makes those requirements easier to meet. However, on‑premises also means you own the operational responsibilities. You must size virtual machines, maintain hypervisor health, and ensure high availability across data centers. You also need to make controllers reachable across WAN segments and design firewall rules appropriately. A common misconception is that on‑premises always costs less; initial capital and staffing overhead, and the need for redundancy across sites, can make it more expensive than expected. When you pick on‑premises, plan for at least two vSmart controllers in separate locations for resilience, ensure vManage has reliable low‑latency access to edge devices, and document operations for certificate renewal and license lifecycle. On‑Premises Deployment: Strengths and Responsibilities means maximum control but increased operational responsibility: plan for sizing, redundancy, and firewalling.. In practical terms, why organizations pick on‑premises and what operational work it requires. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › On‑Premises Deployment
Comparison

Strengths and responsibilities

On‑premises gives control and sovereignty but requires teams to manage infrastructure and redundancy.

Strength: Control
Full control of OS, backups, logging, and security policies.
Responsibility: Ops
You must patch hypervisors, size VMs, and manage cross‑site redundancy.
Practical checklist
  • Plan at least two vSmart controllers across separate sites for HA.
  • Ensure vManage has low‑latency links to the devices it manages.
  • Document certificate renewal and licensing procedures.
Misconception Check

On‑premises is not always cheaper. Consider staff, redundancy, and maintenance when comparing costs.

screens.title: Cloud‑Hosted Deployment Benefits and Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud‑hosted controller deployment moves the operational burden of physical hardware to the cloud provider while allowing you to run vManage, vSmart, and vBond as virtual machines. This model shines when you need rapid scaling, regional availability, or want to avoid maintaining server hardware. A concrete example is placing vBond in a cloud region so remote edge devices behind NAT can reach it without complex on‑premises exposure. But cloud hosting also requires you to consider latency to edge sites, the cloud provider’s network topology, and compliance rules around where data and telemetry are stored. It is a common mistake to assume that cloud hosting removes networking configuration; in practice, you still must open and verify all required ports, set security groups or firewall policies correctly, and size VMs based on device count and telemetry load. When assessing cloud hosting, confirm data residency requirements, estimate VM resources using Cisco sizing guidance, and test latency between cloud controllers and representative branch devices. Cloud‑Hosted Deployment Benefits and Considerations means cloud hosting reduces hardware ops and improves reachability, but verify latency, compliance, and correct networking rules.. In practical terms, when cloud hosting of controllers makes sense and what to check before you launch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Cloud‑Hosted Deployment
Definition

Cloud‑hosted controllers

Controllers run as cloud VMs for scalability and managed availability; still require careful network and security configuration.

Benefit: Scalability
Easily scale VM sizes and rely on cloud availability features.
Consideration: Latency and Compliance
Measure latency to branch devices and check data residency rules before committing.
Practical checks
  • Use provider marketplace images or AMIs to simplify deployment.
  • Open cloud security groups or firewall ports required by SD‑WAN controllers.
  • Run latency tests from representative branches before production cutover.
Key Takeaway

Cloud hosting reduces server ops but still needs network design, sizing, and compliance checks to succeed.

screens.title: Hybrid Deployment Patterns and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid deployments combine on‑premises and cloud hosting to balance control and reachability. A common pattern is to place vManage and vSmart in your private data center for control and policy management while placing vBond in a public cloud or DMZ. The reason is simple: vBond is the initial orchestrator that needs to be reachable by vEdge devices during bootstrap, including those behind NAT. Hosting vBond in the cloud reduces the need to expose on‑prem network edges directly to the internet. For example, you might keep telemetry and configuration state inside your data center while allowing branches to reach vBond in a cloud region for initial authentication. The process to adopt hybrid is deliberate: decide which controllers require data sovereignty, choose cloud regions for reachability, configure secure connectivity between cloud and DC, and verify firewall and NAT behavior. A misconception is thinking hybrid automatically simplifies certificates or licensing; certificates still require correct CN fields and trusted CAs, and licenses must be uploaded to whichever vManage controls the fabric. The core benefit is flexibility: hybrid lets you tune each controller’s placement to operational and regulatory needs.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid Pattern
keyIdea.text: Keep sensitive controllers local and place reachability-critical controllers like vBond in a public cloud to ease branch registration.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Hybrid Deployment
Process Flow

Hybrid deployment steps

  1. Decide which controllers require local data residency.
  2. Place reachability controllers (often vBond) in public cloud or DMZ.
  3. Establish secure connectivity and firewall rules between cloud and DC.
  4. Verify NAT, ports, and certificate CN alignment for all controllers.
Concrete example
A bank keeps vManage and vSmart in private DCs for compliance, while vBond runs in cloud region X so remote retail branches behind NAT can register without complex inbound rules.
Verify that vBond's public IP and system IP are configured correctly in vManage when adding the controller.
Misconception Check

Hybrid does not remove the need for correct certificate CNs, NTP sync, or firewall openings. It only gives placement flexibility.

screens.title: Controller Placement: vManage, vSmart, vBond Principles
screens.narratorSegment: Controller placement is more than geography; it affects control plane latency, redundancy, and the ability for devices to bootstrap. vManage must have reliable, low‑latency connectivity to the vEdge and cEdge devices it configures; if vManage is too distant, configuration pushes and telemetry will be slow or unreliable. vSmart controllers are the policy and control plane engines, and best practice is to run at least two vSmart controllers in different geographic locations or data centers to provide high availability and reduce control path latency. vBond is special: it is the orchestrator that facilitates initial connections and must be reachable by all controllers and edge devices, even those behind NAT. That is why vBond is often placed in a DMZ or cloud. A practical layout would be vManage and vSmart in primary DCs, a second vSmart in a regional site, and vBond in the cloud. A misconception is treating system IP and interface IP as interchangeable. System IP is a unique fabric identifier and must be unique across all devices; duplicates will break fabric operations. Decide placement based on reachability, redundancy, and expected control traffic patterns.

Decide placement based on reachability, redundancy, and expected control traffic patterns.

keyIdea.title: Placement Principle
keyIdea.text: Place controllers to reduce control-plane latency, ensure high availability, and make vBond reachable for device bootstrap.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Controller Placement
Architecture

Placement rules

Design for low latency, redundancy, and reachability. vManage for monitoring, vSmart for control, vBond for orchestration.

vManage
Needs reliable, low‑latency connectivity to devices for configuration and telemetry.
vSmart
Deploy at least two across locations for redundancy and to reduce control path latency.
vBond
Place where it is reachable by all devices, often DMZ or cloud, to help bootstrap edges behind NAT.
Concrete layout
Example: vManage and one vSmart in primary DC, second vSmart in DR site, and vBond in a public cloud to ease branch bootstrap and NAT traversal.
Reminder: system IPs must be unique across all controllers and edges.
Misconception Check

Do not assume a single controller location serves all branches well. Measure latency and design for redundancy.

screens.title: Sizing Controllers: CPU, Memory, and Storage Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Sizing controllers is a capacity planning task that depends on the number of vEdge or cEdge devices, the expected telemetry volume, and the rate of policy changes. Cisco publishes sizing guidance keyed to device counts and throughput; use those guides as your starting point rather than guessing. The practical approach is to categorize expected load: how many edges will register, how frequently will telemetry be collected, and how many concurrent policy pushes will occur. For example, a small lab with a few dozen devices requires modest C P U and memory, while a global fabric with thousands of edges will need multiple controllers with larger VM sizes and disk for telemetry retention. A common mistake is under‑provisioning disk for telemetry and logs; when storage fills, telemetry ingestion and reporting can fail. Another mistake is sizing only for steady‑state and ignoring bursts during mass device provisioning or policy rollout. To mitigate this, plan for headroom, monitor controller metrics after deployment, and be prepared to scale VM resources or add controller instances if telemetry or control tasks lag. Always confirm platform‑specific VM sizes and IOPS for the cloud provider if hosting there.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Controller Sizing
Hierarchy

Sizing principles

Estimate resources from device counts, telemetry volume, and policy change rates. Use Cisco sizing guides as a baseline.

Inputs
Number of devices, expected telemetry retention, throughput, and policy change frequency.
Risks
Under‑provisioned disk or CPU causes telemetry drops and slow policy pushes during mass changes.
Practical guidance
  • Start with vendor sizing tables mapped to device counts.
  • Provision extra headroom for onboarding and policy rollout bursts.
  • If cloud hosted, verify VM IOPS and network performance for telemetry.
Misconception Check

Don't size only for average load. Plan for peaks and telemetry retention to avoid operational surprises.

screens.title: Initial vManage CLI Configuration (Hands‑On Commands)
screens.narratorSegment: The vManage VM requires a small set of initial console commands to make the web interface reachable. After you deploy the VM from an OVA or AMI and log in with default credentials, you enter configuration mode and set the system hostname, management interface IP, default route, and NTP server. For example, you will enter configuration mode, set the hostname to a clear name like vManage‑Prod‑DC1, configure the management interface with the assigned IP address and mask, and remember to use no shutdown so the interface is administratively up. You then set a default route pointing to the gateway and configure an NTP server so certificate validation will succeed later. A concrete walkthrough command sequence is provided visually in the code panel. A common error is forgetting to commit changes or to enable the interface; always end with the commit and‑quit command. After these steps the vManage web UI should be reachable on TCP 8443, at which point you can generate CSRs and continue certificate and license steps. Question to reflect: did I verify NTP and interface state before proceeding to the GUI?

narration.text: The vManage VM requires a small set of initial console commands to make the web interface reachable. After you deploy the VM from an OVA or AMI and log in with default credentials, you enter configuration mode and set the system hostname, management interface IP, default route, and NTP server. For example, you will enter configuration mode, set the hostname to a clear name like vManage‑Prod‑DC1, configure the management interface with the assigned IP address and mask, and remember to use no shutdown so the interface is administratively up. You then set a default route pointing to the gateway and configure an NTP server so certificate validation will succeed later. A concrete walkthrough command sequence is provided visually in the code panel. A common error is forgetting to commit changes or to enable the interface; always end with the commit and‑quit command. After these steps the vManage web UI should be reachable on TCP 8443, at which point you can generate CSRs and continue certificate and license steps. Question to reflect: did I verify NTP and interface state before proceeding to the GUI?

keyIdea.title: CLI Setup
keyIdea.text: Set hostname, configure interface IP and default route, set NTP, and commit changes so the vManage web UI is reachable.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › vManage CLI Setup
Process

Initial CLI commands

Run these commands on the vManage VM console before using the web UI. Remember to commit and verify NTP.

Checklist
  • Enter config mode and set a clear hostname.
  • Assign management interface IP and bring it up with no shutdown.
  • Set default route and an NTP server, then commit changes.
Example CLI sequence
# config t
# system host-name vManage-Prod-DC1
# interface GigabitEthernet0
#  ip address 172.16.1.100 255.255.255.0
#  no shutdown
# exit
# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.1.1
# system ntp server 10.0.0.5
# commit and-quit
After commit, open a browser to vManage IP on TCP 8443 to continue GUI configuration.
Common mistake

Forgetting no shutdown or commit prevents the interface from coming up or the config from applying; verify with show commands after commit.

screens.title: Certificate Management in vManage
screens.narratorSegment: Certificate management is central to SD‑WAN security. vManage generates Certificate Signing Requests which must be signed by a trusted CA—either an internal enterprise CA or a public CA—and then installed back into vManage so it can authenticate other controllers. The process begins in the vManage web UI with the CSR creation and ends with installing the signed certificate and any necessary CA chain. A concrete example: generate a CSR on vManage, submit it to your internal CA, receive the signed certificate and CA chain, then upload both into the vManage certificate manager. This establishes the root of trust used across vManage, vSmart, vBond, and vEdge devices. Common issues include CN mismatches and unsynchronized time. Ensure the certificate common name maps correctly to the system IP or FQDN expected by the fabric and that all devices share reliable NTP sources. A misconception is thinking self‑signed certs are sufficient for production; they will create browser trust issues and potential interoperability problems. Takeaway: use a trusted CA, validate CNs, and confirm NTP synchronization before onboarding devices. Certificate Management in vManage means generate csr from vmanage, sign with a trusted ca, install signed cert and ca chain, and confirm cn and ntp alignment.. In practical terms, generate csrs, have them signed, and install certificates to build trust. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Certificate Management
Process

CSR generation and installation

Create a CSR in vManage, have it signed by a trusted CA, and install the signed certificate and CA chain back into vManage.

Steps
  1. Generate CSR from vManage certificate manager.
  2. Submit CSR to internal or public CA and receive signed cert and chain.
  3. Install signed cert and CA chain in vManage and verify trust.
Concrete example
Generate CSR in the web UI, export CSR file, have your enterprise CA sign it, then import the signed certificate and root/intermediate chain into vManage so the fabric trusts it.
Check that the certificate CN aligns with the system IP or FQDN used by controllers.
Common Mistake

Time drift causes certificate validation failures. Always verify NTP and the certificate validity window before onboarding devices.

screens.title: Licensing in vManage
screens.narratorSegment: Licensing in Cisco SD‑WAN is a subscription model managed within vManage. To activate features and device counts you upload your Smart Account credentials or license files into vManage. The platform uses these credentials to validate entitlements and enable functionality across the fabric. A practical scenario is an operator who has purchased licenses for a specific number of edge devices: they must upload the smart account data so vManage can enforce device capacity and enable licensed features. A common operational step is to confirm the license tier and device counts in the smart account before uploading. Mistakes include uploading incorrect files or not matching license entitlements to the expected device load, which can prevent devices from joining or limit feature availability. After uploading, verify that vManage shows active licenses and that device counters reflect your purchased capacity. If hosting vManage in the cloud, the same licensing steps apply; ensure the vManage instance can reach Cisco licensing endpoints or that license files are used when internet connectivity is restricted. Licensing in vManage means upload smart account credentials or license files in vmanage to activate features and device capacity; verify counters after upload.. In practical terms, upload smart account credentials or license files to enable features and device capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Licensing
Process

Activate licenses in vManage

Upload Smart Account credentials or license files so vManage can enable features and device capacity across the fabric.

Checklist
  • Confirm license tiers and device counts in your Smart Account before upload.
  • Upload credentials or files in vManage licensing section.
  • Verify active licenses and device counters in the UI after upload.
Concrete note
When internet access to Cisco licensing endpoints is restricted, prepare license files in advance and upload them directly to vManage.
Verify device capacity counters match expected registered devices.
Misconception Check

Don't assume licenses apply automatically; you must upload and confirm entitlements in vManage before expecting full feature access.

screens.title: Adding vBond and vSmart Controllers via vManage
screens.narratorSegment: Adding vBond and vSmart controllers into the fabric is performed from vManage and establishes the control plane topology. In the vManage web UI you navigate to Configuration → Devices → Controllers and add entries for vBond and vSmart by providing the controller's system IP and the public IP it uses for communication if it sits behind NAT. The system IP is a unique fabric identifier, distinct from interface IPs, and every device must have a unique system IP. After adding the controller entry, vManage uses the certificate trust and configuration to initiate secure DTLS/TLS connections. A concrete example: when adding vBond in the cloud, add its system IP and the public IP so branch vEdge devices that are NATed can reach it. Common mistakes include entering incorrect public IPs for NATed controllers or duplicating system IPs. After you add controllers, verify that configuration and certificates are exchanged and that tunnels to other controllers establish successfully. Final reflection: confirm unique system IPs and correct public IPs before expecting edge devices to complete bootstrap. Adding vBond and vSmart Controllers via vManage means add controllers in vmanage with unique system ips and reachable public ips for nat scenarios, then verify secure tunnels.. In practical terms, register controllers with system ips and public ips so the fabric can establish secure connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Add controllers in vManage with unique system IPs and reachable public IPs for NAT scenarios, then verify secure tunnels.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Add vBond & vSmart
Process

Onboard controllers via vManage

Provide system IP and public IP (when behind NAT) in the controller form so vManage can establish trust and connections.

Form fields to set
  • System IP (unique fabric identifier)
  • Public IP (used if controller is behind NAT)
  • Controller role selection (vBond or vSmart)
Concrete example
When adding vBond in a cloud region, specify its system IP and the public IP so NATed edges can reach it; vManage will authenticate using installed certificates and initiate connections.
After adding, check controller status and certificate exchange before onboarding edges.
Common Mistake

Entering duplicate system IPs or incorrect public IPs prevents proper tunnel establishment and device bootstrap.

screens.title: Common Mistakes: NTP, Firewall, Certificates, and System IP
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting early deployment problems is mostly about validating a short list of infrastructure assumptions. First, NTP synchronization: certificate validation and secure tunnel negotiation depend on accurate time. If your controllers and edge devices are out of sync you will see certificate invalid errors and failed joins. The fix is to point all components to a reliable NTP source and confirm time alignment. Second, firewall and port configuration: common ports include TCP 8443 for vManage web UI, TCP 12346 and UDP 12346 for controller and edge control channels, and TCP 12345 between vSmart and vBond; blocking these prevents management and tunnels. Verify security groups and firewall rules in cloud and on‑prem equipment. Third, certificate issues: ensure CSRs are generated correctly, signed by a trusted CA, and the certificate CN matches the expected system IP or FQDN. Finally, system IP uniqueness: overlapping system IPs will break fabric identity. A misconception is assuming a browser warning equals a failed fabric; sometimes the browser warns because the cert is self‑signed while the fabric still needs a signed cert to interoperate. Takeaway: check NTP, firewall ports, certificate CNs, and unique system IPs in that order to find most deployment failures quickly.

keyIdea.text: Verify NTP, open required firewall ports, confirm signed certificates and CNs, and ensure unique system IPs to resolve most failures.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Common Mistakes
Troubleshooting

Frequent failure points

Focus on NTP, firewall rules, certificates, and system IP uniqueness to resolve most deployment issues.

NTP Sync
Time drift causes certificate validation errors. Point all controllers and edges to a reliable NTP server.
Firewall/Ports
Open required ports such as TCP 8443 and controller control ports; verify cloud security groups.
Certificates & System IPs
Ensure CSRs and signed certs are installed correctly, CNs match expected system IPs or FQDNs, and each device has a unique system IP to avoid identity conflicts.
When a browser warns about an untrusted cert, check whether the fabric has a signed cert installed for trust, not just browser trust.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist: NTP, ports, certs, system IPs. Order matters: time first, then connectivity, then certificate validation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. Understand the three deployment models—on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, and hybrid—and choose based on control, reachability, and compliance. Controller placement matters: vManage needs low‑latency access to devices, vSmart should be redundant, and vBond should be reachable for bootstrap, often via cloud or DMZ. System IPs are unique fabric identifiers that must not overlap. Certificates and license management are prerequisites for devices to join the fabric: generate CSRs, have them signed by a trusted CA, install certificates and CA chains, and upload license data. Finally, NTP synchronization and correct firewall port configuration resolve the majority of early deployment failures. Keep this checklist handy when you design and build an SD‑WAN fabric so that configuration flows from a validated infrastructure base to an operational fabric. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the choices and early steps that make a Cisco SD‑WAN deployment work. You will learn the tradeoffs between on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, and hybrid controller models, and you will see why controller placement and sizing are practical design decisions, not abstract concepts. We will also walk through the initial vManage virtual machine configuration and the certificate and licensing steps that let controllers and edges form a secure fabric. A concrete example you will encounter is placing vBond in a public cloud to make it reachable by NATed branch devices while keeping vManage inside a private data center for control and monitoring. Common mistakes like unsynchronized clocks, blocked firewall ports, and duplicate system IPs are shown along with how they disrupt trust and device joins. By the end of this chapter you will be able to pick an appropriate deployment model for a given organizational constraint, perform the initial vManage CLI setup, request and install certificates, and add vBond and vSmart into the fabric. Ask yourself: which constraint in your environment makes control plane placement the highest priority?

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing and standing up a Cisco SD‑WAN fabric. First, you will identify and describe the main deployment models—on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, and hybrid—so you can match architecture to operational and regulatory constraints. Second, you will analyze controller placement and sizing: choose where to place vManage, vSmart, and vBond for redundancy, low latency, and reachability, and estimate C P U, memory, and storage needs based on device counts and telemetry. Third, you will perform the initial vManage CLI configuration: set hostname, management interface, default route, and NTP, then access the web UI to continue setup. Finally, you will manage certificates and licensing in vManage and use vManage to add vBond and vSmart into the fabric, establishing trust. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency, and you'll practice a CLI configuration sequence in the hands‑on activity. Keep these objectives in mind as you progress through the lessons; they connect design, configuration, and operational checks into a repeatable workflow.

This continuation of objectives focuses on measurable outcomes and how you will validate them. You will be able to evaluate controller reachability requirements and decide when vBond should be placed in a DMZ or public cloud to support devices behind NAT. You will practice certificate workflows: generate a CSR from vManage, have it signed by an internal or public CA, and install the signed certificate so controllers can authenticate each other. You will also configure licensing in vManage by uploading smart account credentials or license files to activate features and device counts. Finally, you will perform controller onboarding through vManage and confirm that the controllers establish secure tunnels and accept vEdge or cEdge devices. Each item includes a verification milestone so you can test in your lab: for example, verify that the vManage web UI is reachable on TCP 8443 after initial CLI configuration, and that NTP synchronization prevents certificate validation errors. These skills turn design choices into a working fabric that you can operate reliably.

Deployment model selection is the first architectural decision for SD‑WAN controllers and it shapes operational, security, and availability tradeoffs. An on‑premises deployment places vManage, vSmart, and vBond on servers you control in your data center. This gives maximum control and data sovereignty and is sensible where an organization already has robust virtualization and prefers to own its infrastructure. A concrete example: a global enterprise with two main data centers that wants to avoid public cloud dependency will host all controllers on‑premises, leveraging existing virtualization and backup processes. The cloud‑hosted model moves controllers to public cloud VMs. This offers elasticity, managed availability, and reduced hardware operations. For instance, placing vBond or vManage in a cloud region reduces administrative hardware tasks and can simplify reachability for widely dispersed branches. Hybrid mixes both: keep sensitive controllers in your own DC while placing vBond in the cloud to help NATed branch devices find and register with the fabric. A common misconception is that cloud always means better redundancy; in reality, cloud reduces physical hardware management but still requires correct placement and architecture for low latency and regulatory compliance. Takeaway: match the model to control, reachability, and operational skillsets, not to a single buzzword.

On‑premises deployments are chosen when control, privacy, and tight integration with existing infrastructure are priorities. By installing vManage, vSmart, and vBond inside your own data centers you control patching windows, backup strategies, and network segmentation. A practical example is an enterprise that must retain logs and telemetry within its own environment for compliance; hosting controllers locally makes those requirements easier to meet. However, on‑premises also means you own the operational responsibilities. You must size virtual machines, maintain hypervisor health, and ensure high availability across data centers. You also need to make controllers reachable across WAN segments and design firewall rules appropriately. A common misconception is that on‑premises always costs less; initial capital and staffing overhead, and the need for redundancy across sites, can make it more expensive than expected. When you pick on‑premises, plan for at least two vSmart controllers in separate locations for resilience, ensure vManage has reliable low‑latency access to edge devices, and document operations for certificate renewal and license lifecycle. On‑Premises Deployment: Strengths and Responsibilities means maximum control but increased operational responsibility: plan for sizing, redundancy, and firewalling.. In practical terms, why organizations pick on‑premises and what operational work it requires. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cloud‑hosted controller deployment moves the operational burden of physical hardware to the cloud provider while allowing you to run vManage, vSmart, and vBond as virtual machines. This model shines when you need rapid scaling, regional availability, or want to avoid maintaining server hardware. A concrete example is placing vBond in a cloud region so remote edge devices behind NAT can reach it without complex on‑premises exposure. But cloud hosting also requires you to consider latency to edge sites, the cloud provider’s network topology, and compliance rules around where data and telemetry are stored. It is a common mistake to assume that cloud hosting removes networking configuration; in practice, you still must open and verify all required ports, set security groups or firewall policies correctly, and size VMs based on device count and telemetry load. When assessing cloud hosting, confirm data residency requirements, estimate VM resources using Cisco sizing guidance, and test latency between cloud controllers and representative branch devices. Cloud‑Hosted Deployment Benefits and Considerations means cloud hosting reduces hardware ops and improves reachability, but verify latency, compliance, and correct networking rules.. In practical terms, when cloud hosting of controllers makes sense and what to check before you launch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hybrid deployments combine on‑premises and cloud hosting to balance control and reachability. A common pattern is to place vManage and vSmart in your private data center for control and policy management while placing vBond in a public cloud or DMZ. The reason is simple: vBond is the initial orchestrator that needs to be reachable by vEdge devices during bootstrap, including those behind NAT. Hosting vBond in the cloud reduces the need to expose on‑prem network edges directly to the internet. For example, you might keep telemetry and configuration state inside your data center while allowing branches to reach vBond in a cloud region for initial authentication. The process to adopt hybrid is deliberate: decide which controllers require data sovereignty, choose cloud regions for reachability, configure secure connectivity between cloud and DC, and verify firewall and NAT behavior. A misconception is thinking hybrid automatically simplifies certificates or licensing; certificates still require correct CN fields and trusted CAs, and licenses must be uploaded to whichever vManage controls the fabric. The core benefit is flexibility: hybrid lets you tune each controller’s placement to operational and regulatory needs.

Controller placement is more than geography; it affects control plane latency, redundancy, and the ability for devices to bootstrap. vManage must have reliable, low‑latency connectivity to the vEdge and cEdge devices it configures; if vManage is too distant, configuration pushes and telemetry will be slow or unreliable. vSmart controllers are the policy and control plane engines, and best practice is to run at least two vSmart controllers in different geographic locations or data centers to provide high availability and reduce control path latency. vBond is special: it is the orchestrator that facilitates initial connections and must be reachable by all controllers and edge devices, even those behind NAT. That is why vBond is often placed in a DMZ or cloud. A practical layout would be vManage and vSmart in primary DCs, a second vSmart in a regional site, and vBond in the cloud. A misconception is treating system IP and interface IP as interchangeable. System IP is a unique fabric identifier and must be unique across all devices; duplicates will break fabric operations. Decide placement based on reachability, redundancy, and expected control traffic patterns.

Sizing controllers is a capacity planning task that depends on the number of vEdge or cEdge devices, the expected telemetry volume, and the rate of policy changes. Cisco publishes sizing guidance keyed to device counts and throughput; use those guides as your starting point rather than guessing. The practical approach is to categorize expected load: how many edges will register, how frequently will telemetry be collected, and how many concurrent policy pushes will occur. For example, a small lab with a few dozen devices requires modest C P U and memory, while a global fabric with thousands of edges will need multiple controllers with larger VM sizes and disk for telemetry retention. A common mistake is under‑provisioning disk for telemetry and logs; when storage fills, telemetry ingestion and reporting can fail. Another mistake is sizing only for steady‑state and ignoring bursts during mass device provisioning or policy rollout. To mitigate this, plan for headroom, monitor controller metrics after deployment, and be prepared to scale VM resources or add controller instances if telemetry or control tasks lag. Always confirm platform‑specific VM sizes and IOPS for the cloud provider if hosting there.

For example, you will enter configuration mode, set the hostname to a clear name like vManage‑Prod‑DC1, configure the management interface with the assigned IP address and mask, and remember to use no shutdown so the interface is administratively up. You then set a default route pointing to the gateway and configure an NTP server so certificate validation will succeed later. Certificate management is central to SD‑WAN security. vManage generates Certificate Signing Requests which must be signed by a trusted CA—either an internal enterprise CA or a public CA—and then installed back into vManage so it can authenticate other controllers. The process begins in the vManage web UI with the CSR creation and ends with installing the signed certificate and any necessary CA chain. A concrete example: generate a CSR on vManage, submit it to your internal CA, receive the signed certificate and CA chain, then upload both into the vManage certificate manager. This establishes the root of trust used across vManage, vSmart, vBond, and vEdge devices. Common issues include CN mismatches and unsynchronized time. Ensure the certificate common name maps correctly to the system IP or FQDN expected by the fabric and that all devices share reliable NTP sources. A misconception is thinking self‑signed certs are sufficient for production; they will create browser trust issues and potential interoperability problems. Takeaway: use a trusted CA, validate CNs, and confirm NTP synchronization before onboarding devices. Adding vBond and vSmart controllers into the fabric is performed from vManage and establishes the control plane topology. In the vManage web UI you navigate to Configuration → Devices → Controllers and add entries for vBond and vSmart by providing the controller's system IP and the public IP it uses for communication if it sits behind NAT. The system IP is a unique fabric identifier, distinct from interface IPs, and every device must have a unique system IP. After adding the controller entry, vManage uses the certificate trust and configuration to initiate secure DTLS/TLS connections. Troubleshooting early deployment problems is mostly about validating a short list of infrastructure assumptions. First, NTP synchronization: certificate validation and secure tunnel negotiation depend on accurate time. If your controllers and edge devices are out of sync you will see certificate invalid errors and failed joins. The fix is to point all components to a reliable NTP source and confirm time alignment. Second, firewall and port configuration: common ports include TCP 8443 for vManage web UI, TCP 12346 and UDP 12346 for controller and edge control channels, and TCP 12345 between vSmart and vBond; blocking these prevents management and tunnels. Verify security groups and firewall rules in cloud and on‑prem equipment. Third, certificate issues: ensure CSRs are generated correctly, signed by a trusted CA, and the certificate CN matches the expected system IP or FQDN. Finally, system IP uniqueness: overlapping system IPs will break fabric identity. A misconception is assuming a browser warning equals a failed fabric; sometimes the browser warns because the cert is self‑signed while the fabric still needs a signed cert to interoperate. Takeaway: check NTP, firewall ports, certificate CNs, and unique system IPs in that order to find most deployment failures quickly.

Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. Understand the three deployment models—on‑premises, cloud‑hosted, and hybrid—and choose based on control, reachability, and compliance. Controller placement matters: vManage needs low‑latency access to devices, vSmart should be redundant, and vBond should be reachable for bootstrap, often via cloud or DMZ. System IPs are unique fabric identifiers that must not overlap. Certificates and license management are prerequisites for devices to join the fabric: generate CSRs, have them signed by a trusted CA, install certificates and CA chains, and upload license data. Finally, NTP synchronization and correct firewall port configuration resolve the majority of early deployment failures.
